title: The Gang Gets Whacked (2)

jokes.text: Well, then I guess cocaine is weightless, all right?
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie are trying to weigh their cocaine supply and it's not registering on the scale.
jokes.punchline: Frank's deadpan pseudo-scientific conclusion that cocaine must simply be weightless — treating a drug-dealer logistics problem with detached absurdist logic.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny absurdism — Frank applies impeccable deadpan logic to an insane situation. The humor comes from his total refusal to consider the obvious (they've been snorting it). Tight, economical, character-specific.

jokes.text: What are you doing? Cleaning my hands off. What are you, a cat? Use a towel. My mouth's right here.
jokes.setup: Frank asks what Charlie is doing; Charlie says he's cleaning his hands.
jokes.punchline: Charlie reveals he's cleaning his cocaine-covered hands by licking them — 'My mouth's right here' — confirming he is getting high on the supply.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Charlie — his insane but internally logical justification ('my mouth's right here') is exactly his brand of oblivious self-sabotage. The cat comparison adds a quick visual layer.

jokes.text: We have to be very careful, considering our past addictions to glue and crack.
jokes.setup: Frank is lecturing Charlie about not getting high on the supply.
jokes.punchline: Frank casually name-drops glue AND crack as past addictions in one breath, treating them as obvious background facts.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the nonchalance — Frank lists two extremely serious addictions as if reciting a grocery list. 'Glue and crack' as a pair is inherently funny, and the callback rewards regular viewers.

jokes.text: You huff glue every single day. No, I don't. No? Did you have any today?
jokes.setup: Charlie insists he got over his addictions.
jokes.punchline: Frank's simple 'Did you have any today?' implying the obvious answer is yes.
jokes.explanation: The economy here is excellent — Frank doesn't need to say more. The beat lands on implication. Not extraordinary but tightly executed.

jokes.text: Every ho needs his pimp.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dennis are arguing about money — Frank made $1000 from Dennis's services while Dennis sat in the car.
jokes.punchline: Frank's completely straight assertion of the pimp/ho dynamic as if it's a reasonable business arrangement.
jokes.explanation: Frank deploying pimp logic with absolute sincerity is on-brand. Not the most original joke but delivered with the right bluntness.

jokes.text: It's a rich person's drug. There's no danger involved. It's, like, stockbrokers and high-powered business executives.
jokes.setup: Mac/Charlie suggest they need a gun because dealing drugs is dangerous.
jokes.punchline: Frank confidently asserts cocaine is exclusively a rich person's drug with no danger — an absurdly naive position for a man who literally just became a drug dealer.
jokes.explanation: The gap between Frank's confidence and his obvious wrongness is the engine of this joke. His logic is internally coherent and totally insane simultaneously.

jokes.text: Waltz into a board meeting, slap your drugs down on the conference table and be, like, 'Hey, you guys wanna buy drugs? We're drug dealers.'
jokes.setup: Frank says they should go to Center City and sell to professionals.
jokes.punchline: Mac/Charlie's literal visualization of how that would look — an absurd corporate drug deal pitch — delivered with escalating commitment.
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier moments in this stretch — the specificity of 'slap your drugs down on the conference table' and 'We're drug dealers' as an introduction is perfectly absurd. Highly quotable. The characters' cluelessness about criminal enterprise is a core Sunny comedy engine firing well.

jokes.text: Are you saying that's not gonna work? What are you saying? What are you saying exactly?
jokes.setup: Frank appears to genuinely be unable to understand why the board meeting drug pitch wouldn't work.
jokes.punchline: His repeated, increasingly bewildered questions suggest he had completely bought into this plan and cannot process its failure.
jokes.explanation: Functional extension of the previous joke — Frank's genuine confusion adds a beat but doesn't add new comedic information. Decent but not essential.

jokes.text: At least we didn't become prostitutes. I am not a prostitute. I am providing... Let me handle this. Dennis is providing a very important service to lonely people in need.
jokes.setup: Mac tries to find a silver lining comparing their drug dealing to prostitution.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's indignant denial ('I am not a prostitute') followed immediately by Charlie's euphemistic spin that confirms he literally is one.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure here is sharp: Mac's inadvertent comparison → Dennis's pride-driven denial → Charlie's inadvertent confirmation. Dennis's vanity clashing with reality is perfect character work. Charlie's diplomatic reframe making things worse is classic.

jokes.text: Really? So he speaks for you now? No. I was... He doesn't have to speak if he doesn't want to. I don't? Really? No. You leave everything to me.
jokes.setup: Mac challenges whether Frank speaks for Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Dennis begins to push back, Frank tells him he 'doesn't have to speak,' and Dennis — conditioned — genuinely seems relieved by this, asking 'really?' as if permission not to think is a gift.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's growing infantilization is played for deeply uncomfortable laughs here. His 'I don't? Really?' — genuinely relieved to be absolved of agency — is a great character beat that shows how thoroughly Frank has broken him. The pimp/ho dynamic is at its darkest and funniest here.

jokes.text: All you have to do is sit there, relax, have yourself a drink and just keep looking handsome.
jokes.setup: Frank explaining Dennis's role as a male escort.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's instant, contented 'Okay. I like that arrangement' — his narcissism making him perfectly happy being a pretty prop.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's vanity is so total he's essentially happy to be a beautiful object — the joke lands because it's completely true to his character. The punchline is in the acceptance.

jokes.text: Get me a beer, Frank. Oh, no beer. Too many calories. Yep. It's all about keeping this body fit.
jokes.setup: Dennis, now settling into his escort role, asks for a beer.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately controlling his diet for professional reasons, and Dennis complying — establishing the pimp/dependent dynamic at its most absurdly domestic.
jokes.explanation: The Frank/Dennis dynamic is hitting an uncomfortable parody of an abusive controlling relationship, played for comedy. Dennis's cheerful compliance with his own objectification is the dark punchline.

jokes.text: Every time you talk, you weaken the nation.
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to insert himself into mob business.
jokes.punchline: The mob guy's withering dismissal — 'Every time you talk, you weaken the nation' — is a spectacular put-down delivered with total nonchalance.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode and arguably the most quotable. The grandeur of 'you weaken the nation' — not just the room, not just this conversation, but THE NATION — delivered as a casual aside is impeccably constructed. Perfect economy (five words do devastating work), highly original construction, and the contrast between the insult's scale and the casualness of delivery is pitch-perfect. This ranks with Sunny's best one-liners.

jokes.text: Oh! Youse guys got the right idea with these. It's, like, the perfect mix of comfort and wind resistance. They make that in men's?
jokes.setup: Mac encounters the mob guys wearing something (apparently women's activewear or tracksuits).
jokes.punchline: Mac's earnest admiration and 'They make that in men's?' — not realizing or not caring it may be women's clothing, treating wind resistance as a valid fashion criterion.
jokes.explanation: Mac's oblivious machismo paired with genuine fashion envy for what are likely women's clothes is a good character beat. 'Wind resistance' as a sincere fashion priority is the specific absurd detail that elevates it.

jokes.text: I feel like I'm being seriously underutilized here. Look, if you just give me a chance, I could show you how hard I actually am. What? That's right. I'm so hard that people are scared of me. And they should be, 'cause I'll explode all over them.
jokes.setup: Mac is pleading for a chance to prove himself to the mob.
jokes.punchline: His tough-guy speech slides into unintentional sexual innuendo ('I'll explode all over them') while he remains completely oblivious.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny innuendo-by-obliviousness. Mac's desperation to seem tough produces increasingly absurd statements. 'Explode all over them' as an accidental double entendre is the peak. Works better in performance than on page.

jokes.text: What? What are you talkin' about, your dick? My dick? No, I'm talkin' about my brute force and my catlike reflexes.
jokes.setup: The mob guy is horrified/confused by Mac's 'explode all over them' statement.
jokes.punchline: The mob guy assumes Mac is talking about his genitals; Mac is mortified and pivots to 'catlike reflexes' as if that's more dignified.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the innuendo above. The punch is the reveal that Mac's alternative explanation ('catlike reflexes') is equally absurd. Lands as a solid secondary laugh.

jokes.text: You know what? I think someone just earned themselves a nickname. Really? What? Yep. From now on, you'll be known as Pussy Hands.
jokes.setup: Mac tries to redeem himself by emphasizing he has 'hands like a cat.'
jokes.punchline: The mob guy bestows the nickname 'Pussy Hands' — which Mac cannot escape for the rest of the episode.
jokes.explanation: The nickname is perfectly constructed — it weaponizes Mac's own language against him, sticks immediately, and becomes a running gag for the rest of the episode. The setup earns it, the name itself is funny, and the institutional way the mob guy declares it ('From now on, you'll be known as...') adds ceremony to the humiliation. Strong joke.

jokes.text: I'd like to go on record saying I don't like Pussy Hands. But Cougar Hands would be good.
jokes.setup: Mac has just been given the nickname 'Pussy Hands.'
jokes.punchline: He formally objects but immediately offers 'Cougar Hands' as an acceptable alternative — missing the point entirely while trying to negotiate his humiliation.
jokes.explanation: Mac's negotiation is perfect character work — he doesn't reject the concept of being named after a cat, just objects to the specific diminutive. 'Cougar Hands' as a preferred alternative reveals he thinks the problem is prestige, not the substance of the insult. Great beat.

jokes.text: Here's to you, Pussy Hands. That's great. It's settled. Hey, Pussy Hands, go wash my car.
jokes.setup: Mac has tried to negotiate his nickname.
jokes.punchline: The mob guys toast him, declare it settled, and immediately put him back to washing the car — the nickname has upgraded nothing about his status.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the running gag — the ceremony of the toast followed immediately by 'go wash my car' is the right deflating button.

jokes.text: How about Jaguar Hands? Nah. Leopard Hands? Nah. Panther Hands. Nah. Goddamn it.
jokes.setup: Mac is still trying to renegotiate his nickname.
jokes.punchline: He runs through progressively prestigious big-cat alternatives, each shot down with a flat 'Nah,' until he gives up.
jokes.explanation: The list joke works because it escalates through the big-cat prestige hierarchy while the flat 'Nah' deflates each attempt identically. Mac's 'Goddamn it' is the perfect button. The rhythm of this sequence is impeccably timed.

jokes.text: Go get your saucer of milk, honey. He does have gorgeous hands though.
jokes.setup: Mac has exhausted his big-cat negotiation options.
jokes.punchline: The mob guys send him off with 'saucer of milk' (leaning into the cat metaphor) then one of them adds the sincere aside that he does have gorgeous hands.
jokes.explanation: The 'saucer of milk' is a solid button, but the real laugh is the sincere mob-guy aside about gorgeous hands — the unexpected softness from a hard man, delivered as a genuine compliment, is a great subversion.

jokes.text: Remember the country club, with the jockeys? This about the horse, Charlie? It is about the horse. Goddamn it. I'm pretty sure those jockeys are raping that horse.
jokes.setup: Charlie suggests going to the country club.
jokes.punchline: Dee's immediate recognition ('this about the horse') and Charlie's sincere concern about jockeys 'raping' the horse — a completely unhinged callback delivered as a reasonable grievance.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's singular obsession with this horse, Dee's weary recognition of the pattern, and the specific accusation ('raping that horse') delivered as a genuine moral concern is very Sunny. The sincerity is the joke.

jokes.text: They're raping the shit out of it.
jokes.setup: Charlie has just said the jockeys are raping the horse.
jokes.punchline: He immediately escalates — 'They're raping the shit out of it' — adding emphasis as though the degree of the alleged horse-raping is an important detail to communicate.
jokes.explanation: The escalation adds nothing logically but everything comedically — Charlie's need to quantify the horse-raping is the joke. The vulgarity is in service of his sincere outrage.

jokes.text: These people are revved up. They're in fifth gear, and we're stuck in first. We need to boost our r.p.m.'s.
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie are frustrated that no one will engage with their street drug sales.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's completely automotive metaphor for their need to get more energetic — treating drug-dealing failure as an RPM problem.
jokes.explanation: Decent bit of Charlie pseudo-logic. The RPM metaphor is funny but the joke doesn't reach its full potential — it's more of a bridge to the cocaine-on-gums bit than a standalone.

jokes.text: A little dip into our Bolivian marching powder, then we're back on the street. Not in your nose. That's how you become a drug addict. Rub it all over your gums, Dee. All over your gums.
jokes.setup: Charlie suggests they use their own product to get more energetic.
jokes.punchline: His completely sincere advice that rubbing cocaine on your gums is NOT how you become an addict — the nose being the dangerous delivery method — is spectacularly wrong advice delivered with total authority.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's confident drug misinformation is impeccably character-specific. His distinction between 'nose = addiction' and 'gums = fine' is the kind of internally logical nonsense that only he would believe and that's also sort of how drug novices might actually think. 'All over your gums' repeated with authority is very funny.

jokes.text: It's like my mouth is no longer a part of my head. I kind of feel nothing, but it feels so good.
jokes.setup: Dee has just rubbed cocaine on her gums for the first time.
jokes.punchline: Her immediate, rapturous description of numbing — 'my mouth is no longer a part of my head' — delivered with wonder and delight.
jokes.explanation: Dee's innocent delight at cocaine numbing is funny because she sounds like someone discovering a great new appetizer. The disconnect between the drug and her suburban-mom-discovering-novelty energy is the joke.

jokes.text: Keep reapplying every 10 to 15 minutes. That's what I've been doing.
jokes.setup: Charlie is coaching Dee on cocaine gum-rubbing technique.
jokes.punchline: His admission that he's been doing this every 10-15 minutes — revealing he's been systematically getting high on the supply the entire time.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to the episode's opening — Charlie has been doing exactly what Frank told him not to do, with his own systematic methodology. His casual self-revelation is the punchline.

jokes.text: They let you become a priest again, huh? Congratulations. It's the reverend. Keep your head up, Reverend. Keep the faith. Bless you. Oh. Yikes. I get it.
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie (now coked up) run into Cricket on the street — who is clearly homeless and in terrible condition.
jokes.punchline: Charlie cheerfully assumes Cricket has been reinstated as a priest; when Cricket's true state becomes apparent, Dee's 'Oh. Yikes.' is the perfect understated reaction.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's coke-fueled obliviousness to Cricket's obvious homelessness is funny, as is his upbeat priestly encouragement ('Keep the faith') that lands as satire. Dee's dawning 'Oh. Yikes.' is the best beat — small and perfect.

jokes.text: Actually, it's the opposite of great, Charlie. It's one of the darkest times of my life. Is it? Is it? That makes sense. Yes.
jokes.setup: Cricket explains his homelessness is terrible; Charlie responds 'That's great.'
jokes.punchline: Cricket's heartfelt correction ('it's the opposite of great') and Charlie's completely unbothered 'Is it? Is it? That makes sense.' — total indifference dressed up as engagement.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's faux-empathetic 'Is it? Is it?' with zero actual concern is a great beat — he's going through the emotional motions without any of the substance. The rhythm of the exchange is tight.

jokes.text: But the good thing is that you must know a lot of drug addicts. Yes. I was actually attacked by a couple last night. Almost got stabbed. Really? That's great. Did you? Did you really? Wonderful, Cricket. Then you can help us sell our cocaine.
jokes.setup: Charlie is 'sympathizing' with Cricket's horror stories about homeless life.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's consistent reframing of Cricket's victimization as useful business intelligence — getting stabbed is 'wonderful' because it proves he has the right social network.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's sociopathic optimism about Cricket's trauma is very Sunny — the worse Cricket's situation sounds, the more Charlie sees opportunity. 'Wonderful, Cricket' as a response to 'I was almost stabbed' is a great dark laugh.

jokes.text: We would do it, but we're not street urchins. Yeah, man. Yeah. Know what I mean? But you. They would buy drugs from a street urchin like yourself. You got the 'street urchin' thing goin' on.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee are recruiting Cricket to sell drugs for them.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's repeated use of 'street urchin' as both an accurate descriptor and a sales qualification — 'you got the street urchin thing going on' as a compliment.
jokes.explanation: The term 'street urchin' is funny because Charlie deploys it clinically, as though it's a professional credential. The escalating usage is good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Please stop calling me a street urchin. I'm not a street urchin. I was a priest. I have a master's in theology. That was then. This is now. What good's it doing you?
jokes.setup: Cricket protests his 'street urchin' label by citing his credentials.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's pragmatic dismissal — 'That was then. This is now. What good's it doing you?' — is a devastating philosophical point delivered without any empathy.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's brutal pragmatism — 'What good's it doing you?' — applied to a master's in theology from a homeless former priest is a great dark comedy line. The economy is excellent and the character specificity is high — only Charlie could deliver this dismissal so earnestly.

jokes.text: I guess Charlie and I didn't see you sitting atop your homeless ivory tower.
jokes.setup: Cricket insists he's trying to get his life back on track and won't sell drugs.
jokes.punchline: Dee's withering 'homeless ivory tower' — a perfect oxymoron that skewers Cricket's moral high ground given his current circumstances.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Homeless ivory tower' is a genuinely brilliant construction — it perfectly captures the absurdity of a homeless man refusing to participate in drug dealing on moral grounds. The oxymoron lands hard, it's highly quotable, and it's exactly what this show does best: a character making an incisive, cruel point that is also completely correct.

jokes.text: Can I stop this little lovers' quarrel? You're not fooling anybody, Cricket. Clearly, the two of you have strong feelings for each other and you're letting that get in the way of a good business deal here.
jokes.setup: Cricket and Dee are arguing; Charlie intervenes.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's confident assertion that their animosity is unresolved sexual tension framed as a business problem — using it as a negotiation lever.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's ability to identify and weaponize people's weaknesses while completely ignoring his own involvement in Cricket's downfall is good character work. The lovers' quarrel framing is predictable but serviceable.

jokes.text: I'll let you stay at Dee's place. No. Till you're back up on your feet. Dee's place? Yeah. You two alone, together. One thing could lead to another. You never know.
jokes.setup: Charlie is using Cricket's apparent feelings for Dee as a bargaining chip.
jokes.punchline: He offers Dee's apartment as Cricket's payment — without telling Dee — implying they might hook up, treating Cricket's hopeless crush as a recruitment incentive.
jokes.explanation: Charlie volunteering Dee's apartment and romantic life without her consent is a good bit of Sunny selfishness. Cricket's vulnerability making him an easy mark is appropriately dark.

jokes.text: You think she still likes me? Yeah. I wasn't sure. I know we have sort of a sexual tension. No, no, no. You guys got your own thing going on. I gotta take a cut now, Cricket. We're working together.
jokes.setup: Cricket is momentarily hopeful about Dee.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately pivots to 'I gotta take a cut now, Cricket' — he's been manufacturing Cricket's hope purely to extract a business arrangement, and the pivot is instant and cold.
jokes.explanation: The speed of the pivot from Cricket's hopeful romantic question to 'I gotta take a cut now' is perfectly sociopathic. Charlie's manipulation is laid completely bare in one line. Good dark comedy beat.

jokes.text: Jesus Christ, Frank. I can't believe you had that thing made. Every pimp has a chalice. This one is the shit.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals he has had a custom pimp chalice made.
jokes.punchline: Frank's matter-of-fact assertion that all pimps require a chalice and his is simply superior — treating a prop pimp chalice as a standard professional tool.
jokes.explanation: Frank's total commitment to pimp aesthetics — including commissioning a custom chalice — while simultaneously refusing to pay off the mob is a great character detail. 'This one is the shit' delivered with pride is very Frank Reynolds.

jokes.text: You spend a shitload of money on a chalice you're just gonna eat cereal out of but you won't bail us out by paying the mob?
jokes.setup: Frank has the chalice; Dennis and Mac still owe the mob money.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's exasperated logic — the chalice is apparently just for cereal, making the fiscal irresponsibility even more absurd.
jokes.explanation: The cereal detail is the comedic payload — Frank's magnificent pimp chalice has the domestic use of a cereal bowl, making his refusal to pay the mob with the same money even more absurd. Sharp line.

jokes.text: Aw, you gotta be kid... Dude, she's, like, a hundred years old. Sixty-eight tops. That's still extremely old. Well, I'm not kissing that.
jokes.setup: Frank points out Dennis's client for the evening.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's horror; Frank's correction ('Sixty-eight tops') stated as a reasonable improvement; Dennis's rule-setting ('I'm not kissing that').
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'Sixty-eight tops' as a reassurance is funny because it's not actually reassuring. Dennis's professional line-drawing ('not kissing that') while presumably fine with everything else is dark character comedy.

jokes.text: This time, nothing with the ass. That got really weird last time. What are you talkin' about? You didn't set up that ass play on the last one? No. I never set up any ass play.
jokes.setup: Dennis is setting rules for his escort work; mentions no ass play.
jokes.punchline: Frank's revelation that he's apparently been arranging ass play for Dennis without his knowledge — 'You didn't set up that ass play on the last one?' — meaning it happened to Dennis without his consent or knowledge.
jokes.explanation: This is a great piece of escalating horror — Frank has apparently been booking extras for Dennis without telling him, meaning things happened to Dennis that Frank arranged that Dennis didn't know about. The reveal is structured perfectly: Dennis's prohibition leads to Frank's innocent inquiry which reveals the dark backstory. Very Sunny.

jokes.text: All right. Well. I wanna set up a doctor's appointment anyway just to be... just to be safe.
jokes.setup: Frank has just revealed he may have set up unknown sexual acts for Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's quietly horrified decision to see a doctor 'just to be safe' — a massive understatement for what the revelation implies.
jokes.explanation: The understated horror of 'just to be safe' as Dennis processes what Frank may have let happen to him is a great button. The trailing off ('just to be...') before the repetition sells the dawning dread.

jokes.text: Hypothetically speaking here... do you think you could teach a horse to sit on a barstool and drink beer? I don't know. Maybe. Would you hypothetically pay really good money to see that?
jokes.setup: Charlie opens with 'hypothetically speaking' as though the horse question requires legal cover.
jokes.punchline: The horse barstool beer idea, delivered as a genuinely exciting business proposition, while Mac and others are preoccupied with actual life-or-death problems.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's 'hypothetically' framing of the horse plan is perfect — it implies he knows it's insane but isn't going to let that stop him. The horse-on-barstool-drinking-beer image is specifically absurd. Mac's 'maybe' is a great beat — he's genuinely considering it.

jokes.text: Is this about bringing a horse back to the bar? That is completely insane. I'm askin' hypothetical questions here. I'm sorry. I'm a little preoccupied with worrying about being killed by the mob because a homeless priest ran off with all of our drugs. Sure. Sure.
jokes.setup: Mac sees through Charlie's 'hypothetical.'
jokes.punchline: Mac's exasperated summary of their situation — 'being killed by the mob because a homeless priest ran off with all of our drugs' — stated as the actually insane reality while Charlie just says 'Sure. Sure.' dismissively.
jokes.explanation: Mac's deadpan enumeration of their absurd actual situation — 'a homeless priest ran off with all of our drugs' — stated so matter-of-factly is the joke. Charlie's breezy 'Sure. Sure.' dismissal of imminent death in favor of horse business is very funny.

jokes.text: It's Rickety Cricket. It's Rickety Cricket. It's Rickety Cricket.
jokes.setup: Someone knocks on the door and says 'Matthew Mara'; the gang doesn't recognize the name.
jokes.punchline: The simultaneous realization that it's Rickety Cricket — delivered three times with escalating excitement — treating him as a beloved figure despite having destroyed his life.
jokes.explanation: The triple delivery of 'It's Rickety Cricket' with mounting joy from people who have ruined this man's life is a good dark-comedy beat. The excitement for a man they're exploiting is appropriately awful.

jokes.text: Hey, is there a dream catcher above your bed?
jokes.setup: Cricket arrives at Dee's apartment for the first time.
jokes.punchline: His immediate observation of a dream catcher above Dee's bed — implying it's exactly the kind of embarrassing personal item that reveals more about Dee than she'd like.
jokes.explanation: The dream catcher works as a visual character detail — it's exactly what an uncool person who thinks they're cool would have. Dee's embarrassment is implied. Quick and effective.

jokes.text: Shit, shit, shit! Holy shit! Look at all that money. That is a huge wad of money. This is more money than we make at the bar. I have never seen this much money in one spot.
jokes.setup: Cricket reveals he sold all the drugs and hands over a massive stack of money.
jokes.punchline: The gang's completely unhinged reaction — a cascade of profanity and financial amazement — to an amount of money that reveals just how poor and unsuccessful they actually are.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the revelation of their poverty — the gang has 'never seen this much money in one spot,' which tells you everything about their financial situation. The escalating profanity is functional if not exceptional.

jokes.text: I can get a horse. You're not gonna get a horse, Charlie. We can have some coke then. She likes Swiss! I knew it! I pictured Swiss.
jokes.setup: The gang is planning what to do with extra money.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's horse plan is dismissed but Dee's Swiss cheese revelation ('She likes Swiss! I knew it!') lands as a bizarrely specific and passionate victory — suggesting Charlie has been debating this horse's cheese preferences.
jokes.explanation: The 'I pictured Swiss' line is a great absurdist beat — Charlie has apparently been mentally modeling this horse's cheese preferences. It's a specific, weird, throwaway detail that reveals a lot about how Charlie's brain works. Highly character-specific.

jokes.text: But you guys said it was a onetime thing. We say things all day. We say words all the time. We said so many things.
jokes.setup: Cricket protests being sent back out to deal more drugs after they said it was a one-time thing.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's magnificent dismissal — 'We say things all day. We say words all the time. We said so many things.' — as a philosophical position that their previous commitments mean nothing.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode and among the best in Sunny's catalogue. 'We say things all day. We say words all the time. We said so many things.' is a perfectly constructed dismissal of the entire concept of keeping promises. The escalating generality — from 'things' to 'words' to 'so many things' — is structurally excellent. Highly quotable, completely character-specific to Charlie, and a genuinely original construction of an argument.

jokes.text: I was thinking maybe I'd curl up on that bed of Dee's and I'd sleep with the bear.
jokes.setup: Cricket is exhausted and wants to rest.
jokes.punchline: His specific mention of 'sleep with the bear' — a stuffed animal presumably on Dee's bed — is both pathetic and oddly sweet, and reveals that Dee has a teddy bear on her bed.
jokes.explanation: The bear detail is funny on two levels — it reveals Cricket's total exhaustion and vulnerability, and it reveals Dee has a stuffed animal, which is an appropriately embarrassing detail. Good layered joke.

jokes.text: Every good dealer keeps a head stash. No. Dip your finger in there. I can't. Let's speed you up.
jokes.setup: Cricket is exhausted and doesn't want to go back out.
jokes.punchline: Charlie producing his 'head stash' — a drug dealer's emergency reserve — and immediately using it to manipulate Cricket back into service by getting him high.
jokes.explanation: Charlie drugging his asset to keep him working is appropriately dark. 'Let's speed you up' is a chilling line delivered with complete casualness. The power dynamic here is very Sunny — the gang treating Cricket as a resource to be managed.

jokes.text: Where am I having dinner tonight, Frank? I'm kind of in the mood for Asian fusion. No more dinners. We're going straight to banging from now on.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks about dinner plans — his only remaining pretense of being a 'companion' rather than a prostitute.
jokes.punchline: Frank's blunt 'No more dinners. We're going straight to banging from now on' — stripping away the last euphemism.
jokes.explanation: Frank's escalating reduction of Dennis's professional euphemisms to blunt reality is consistent and funny. 'Asian fusion' as Dennis's last grasp at dignity before 'we're going straight to banging' is a good contrast.

jokes.text: I'm a handsome companion who goes to nice dinners with fancy women and who has rules about what he'll do. What happened to the rules, Frank? It says right here 'No Rules.'
jokes.setup: Dennis insists he's not a prostitute and has rules; Frank shows him the advertisement.
jokes.punchline: Frank's ad literally says 'No Rules' — directly contradicting Dennis's entire self-conception.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's carefully constructed self-image ('handsome companion with rules') against Frank's ad ('No Rules') is a good joke. Dennis's delusion is the engine of the entire subplot.

jokes.text: I'm walkin' from this. What the hell, dude? I'm knocking some sense into you, Dennis. This is all you got. Dude, why do you keep hitting me? Don't talk back to me! Okay. Sorry.
jokes.setup: Dennis tries to leave; Frank physically stops him.
jokes.punchline: Frank's abusive relationship behavior — hitting Dennis, telling him 'this is all you got' — and Dennis immediately capitulating with 'Okay. Sorry.' — a full abusive relationship dynamic played entirely for dark comedy.
jokes.explanation: The Frank/Dennis dynamic has fully become a parody of an abusive pimp relationship, which is played completely straight. Dennis's instant 'Okay. Sorry.' is appropriately horrifying and funny. The show committing to the dark logic of the scenario is what makes it work.

jokes.text: Look, I'm gonna get you out of this. It's you and me against the world. I'm not gonna let anything bad happen to you. You promise? I promise. And, hey, I don't wanna hit you, baby. So please don't make me, okay? You're my one and only.
jokes.setup: Frank tries to reassure Dennis after hitting him.
jokes.punchline: Frank's speech is a textbook abuser's post-violence reassurance: 'I don't wanna hit you, baby. So please don't make me.' — delivered as though it's loving comfort.
jokes.explanation: 'I don't wanna hit you, baby. So please don't make me' is a devastating line — it's the classic abuser's reframe delivered with complete sincerity. The show committing to the horror of this relationship is exactly the kind of dark comedy Sunny excels at. Dennis's 'You promise?' and 'Okay' are equally great.

jokes.text: Is it any crazier than having a dog that bites or sheds? Or a cat that poops in a box while it's biting you? While it's biting you?
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie he can't get a horse because it's crazy.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's comparative argument that a horse is no crazier than pets — his description of a cat 'pooping in a box while it's biting you' as though simultaneous defecation and assault is the standard cat experience.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's pro-horse argument is great absurdist logic — he reframes the horse as a reasonable pet by describing cats and dogs in the most uncharitable possible terms. 'Pooping in a box while it's biting you' is specific and funny, and Mac's echo ('While it's biting you?') signals the audience reaction perfectly.

jokes.text: Cricket! There you are! I'm workin' on my moves. What moves? For my musical. I'm writing a musical. It's about life on the streets. Archangel has to live on the streets and fight crime.
jokes.setup: The gang finds Cricket — who was supposed to be selling drugs — doing something else entirely.
jokes.punchline: Cricket has abandoned drug-dealing to work on a musical about a street-fighting archangel, and is developing choreography on the street.
jokes.explanation: Cricket's descent has taken a creative turn — a homeless man on cocaine developing a musical about a crime-fighting archangel is a spectacular character moment. 'Archangel has to live on the streets and fight crime' is a perfect absurdist detail. The specificity is what elevates it.

jokes.text: Spent the money on these sweetass kettledrums. Look at these. Those are trash cans. Trash cans, Cricket! These are trash cans? Then why do they sound like this?
jokes.setup: Cricket reveals he spent the drug money on 'kettledrums' for his musical.
jokes.punchline: They're trash cans. Cricket is genuinely baffled to learn this, and defends them by playing them — as though the sound quality justifies the purchase.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'These are trash cans? Then why do they sound like this?' with the implied drumming is a perfect comedic beat — Cricket's coke-fueled confusion about what trash cans are, combined with his genuine artistic defense of them, is both absurd and strangely sympathetic. The structure is excellent: setup (kettledrums), reversal (trash cans), Cricket's defense. The beat where he plays them is an implied visual gag that lands enormous.

jokes.text: No. No, no, no, no. I did some too. We can see that!
jokes.setup: The gang accuses Cricket of spending the drug money on trash cans.
jokes.punchline: Cricket clarifies he also did some of the cocaine, and the gang responds 'We can see that!' — meaning his behavior has made it obvious he's high.
jokes.explanation: Good beat that lands on a simple reaction line. 'We can see that' is a solid straight-man response to cricket's oblivious confession.

jokes.text: I still gotta write the seventh act. It's kinda all up here.
jokes.setup: The gang is yelling at Cricket about the drug money.
jokes.punchline: Cricket's total non-sequitur — his musical has a seventh act, and it exists only in his cocaine-addled mind — delivered as a reasonable explanation for why he needs the remaining drugs.
jokes.explanation: 'I still gotta write the seventh act' is funny on multiple levels — a seven-act musical is absurd, it's entirely in his head, and he's citing it as a legitimate justification for more cocaine. 'It's kinda all up here' as he points to his head is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Watch the crack addicts though. They will cut you.
jokes.setup: Cricket is heading back out with his trash can kettledrums.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's completely casual safety tip about crack addicts cutting you — delivered as normal street-safety advice.
jokes.explanation: Perfect example of Sunny deadpan — Charlie's most maternal advice to Cricket is 'watch out for crack addicts with knives,' delivered as casually as 'wear a coat.' The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: It's $200 for the first hour, and a hundred and fifty every hour after that. Unless you want him to act like he's enjoying it. Then it's a little extra.
jokes.setup: Frank is negotiating Dennis's rates with a client.
jokes.punchline: 'Unless you want him to act like he's enjoying it. Then it's a little extra.' — implying Dennis cannot convincingly fake enthusiasm and that authentic performance is a premium service.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The implication — that Dennis's default state is not enjoying himself and that enthusiasm costs extra — is both a great joke about sex work economics and a devastating character note about Dennis. The phrasing 'act like he's enjoying it' is elegant and the structure is clean. Frank's completely businesslike delivery of this information is pitch-perfect.

jokes.text: You like ass play? He'll do anything with the ass. I never said... I wasn't gonna tell...
jokes.setup: Frank is negotiating with a client; Dennis can apparently overhear.
jokes.punchline: Frank offers ass play as a service despite Dennis's explicit earlier prohibition, and Dennis's horrified, sputtering protest ('I never said... I wasn't gonna tell...') reveals he's hearing this in real time.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to Dennis's ass-play rules — Frank ignores them immediately and in the worst possible context. Dennis's sputtering non-protest ('I wasn't gonna tell...') implies he was about to stay silent before catching himself. Great dark callback.

jokes.text: Forgive me for speaking out of line here, but I don't think I'm being properly utilized within the organization. I've tried to be eager and work with a smile, but I'm not making any forward progress.
jokes.setup: Mac is approaching the mob boss to make his case for advancement.
jokes.punchline: Mac's corporate HR-speak — 'properly utilized,' 'forward progress,' 'work with a smile' — applied to a criminal organization, as though he's doing a performance review with a mob boss.
jokes.explanation: Mac applying professional development language to mob advancement is a great joke — the incongruity between HR-speak and organized crime is well-exploited. 'Work with a smile' in a mob context is particularly good.

jokes.text: What is important is that I get out on those streets and start doing some gangster shit. There's gotta be a union boss I can put the squeeze on. Or a truck I can hijack, right?
jokes.setup: Mac is petitioning the mob boss for real gangster work.
jokes.punchline: His specific examples — 'a union boss I can put the squeeze on' or 'a truck I can hijack' — are drawn from movie mob clichés, suggesting Mac's entire concept of organized crime comes from pop-culture.
jokes.explanation: Mac's mob vocabulary lifted entirely from movies is a good joke. 'Put the squeeze on' and 'hijack a truck' as his specific examples reveal a man who has watched The Sopranos and thinks he knows how this works.

jokes.text: I need you to go over to my house and take care of my wife. You mean, like, rub her out? No. Oh. You want me to bang her? I'm sorry. No! What the hell is wrong with you? Why would you say that? Communication problem.
jokes.setup: Don Sal asks Mac to 'take care of his wife' as a favor.
jokes.punchline: Mac interprets 'take care of' as either murder or sex in that order — exhausting both wrong interpretations before Don Sal can finish his actual meaning. 'Communication problem' as Mac's summary is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection well-executed — 'rub her out' then 'bang her' as Mac's two interpretations of 'take care of' cover both mobster clichés. The structure is clean: two wrong guesses, escalating Don Sal's horror, capped by Mac's breezy 'Communication problem.' Good joke, well-structured.

jokes.text: Sounds shady. I'm in.
jokes.setup: Don Sal says he needs Mac to do him a 'personal favor.'
jokes.punchline: Mac's instant moral calculus — shadiness = participation — is a one-line character summary.
jokes.explanation: 'Sounds shady. I'm in.' is an exceptional line for its economy. Five words that perfectly encapsulate Mac's character — he's not interested in legitimate work, moral ambiguity is the draw. This is the kind of throwaway line that becomes a show's signature.

jokes.text: Goddamn mafia!
jokes.setup: Mac has just been assigned to watch the mob boss's wife — essentially babysitting, not gangster work.
jokes.punchline: Mac's exasperated 'Goddamn mafia!' — realizing the mob is as bureaucratic and boring as any employer.
jokes.explanation: Good button on the mob job sequence. Mac wanted to be a gangster and got assigned to escort duty. The frustration is relatable and the line is economical.

jokes.text: No, Mac, you have to separate yourself from the way they look. Frank says that the only thing that matters in this game is cash.
jokes.setup: Mac is horrified to find Dennis about to sleep with an elderly woman.
jokes.punchline: Dennis has fully internalized pimp logic — quoting Frank as an authority on 'this game' — a full ideological conversion in a few hours.
jokes.explanation: Dennis citing Frank as a philosophical authority on sex work is appropriately dark — he's been fully Stockholm-syndromed in the span of one episode. 'This game' is perfectly pimp-speak.

jokes.text: Frank, he cannot bang this woman. It's the mob boss's wife. What do you think she's gonna do, call her husband and say she's banging a whore?
jokes.setup: Mac discovers the woman Dennis is about to sleep with is the mob boss's wife.
jokes.punchline: Frank's confident logic — a mob boss's wife would never report sleeping with a prostitute to her husband — which is Frank's reasoning for why this is safe.
jokes.explanation: Frank's logic is internally sound and also catastrophically wrong — a great example of his confident wrongness being the engine of disaster. The punchline structure works well.

jokes.text: Dennis, up those stairs. Dennis, don't do it. He's got you brainwashed. Go! Dennis! Stay! Go! Get up there! Now! Stay! Stay! Stay!
jokes.setup: Frank and Mac are trying to get Dennis to go upstairs (to sleep with the mob boss's wife) or leave respectively.
jokes.punchline: The 'Go!/Stay!' battle reduces Dennis to a confused dog being given conflicting commands — culminating in Mac's repeated 'Stay! Stay! Stay!' as though training an animal.
jokes.explanation: The escalating Go!/Stay! sequence is good physical/verbal comedy — Dennis being reduced to a confused pet is the implied visual. Mac's 'Stay! Stay! Stay!' is an absurd but earned escalation.

jokes.text: You're gonna get us killed! Stop! Stop! Stop! Please stop hitting me so I can think for a second.
jokes.setup: Frank and Mac are physically fighting over Dennis's fate.
jokes.punchline: Mac's plea to 'please stop hitting me so I can think for a second' — his priority in a physical altercation is not to defend himself but to have a moment of cognitive clarity.
jokes.explanation: The phrasing is oddly polite and logical for someone being hit, which is the joke. 'So I can think for a second' as the stated purpose for stopping the hitting is good.

jokes.text: You see? This is bad. You got him thinking for himself again. What the hell are you doing, whore? Get back upstairs.
jokes.setup: Mac's argument has caused Dennis to hesitate.
jokes.punchline: Frank's irritation that Dennis is 'thinking for himself again' — framing independent thought as a problem Frank needs to manage — and his immediate pivot to 'Get back upstairs, whore.'
jokes.explanation: 'You got him thinking for himself again' as a complaint is the core absurdism here — Frank sees Dennis's autonomy as a malfunction. It's a great line in context.

jokes.text: What about you, Pussy Hands? Me? Oh, no. I would never sleep with you. You're gross.
jokes.setup: The mob boss's wife turns her attention to Mac after Dennis walks out.
jokes.punchline: Mac's instant, emphatic rejection — 'Oh, no. I would never sleep with you. You're gross.' — is funny because his primary concern is apparently not offense but clarity.
jokes.explanation: The 'Pussy Hands' nickname being used by the mob boss's wife is a good callback. Mac's reaction — not polite refusal but emphatic 'You're gross' — is great character comedy. The running gag payoff works well.

jokes.text: Last taste. Last taste. One more. That's it. Last one. That's it because we're almost out of it. We can't do this.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee keep saying 'last taste' while continuing to do cocaine.
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'last taste / last one / that's it' ritual — clearly cycling through it — is a perfect parody of addiction's self-bargaining, with neither character believing what they're saying.
jokes.explanation: The self-bargaining of 'last one' repeated multiple times is a great comedic truth about addiction — everyone in the room understands exactly what's happening. Well-observed and efficiently executed.

jokes.text: I'm gonna cut it with flour. I don't think the mob's gonna know the difference. You sure that's gonna work? People do it all the time. I think this will trick 'em.
jokes.setup: They've used most of the cocaine and need to return it to the mob.
jokes.punchline: Dee's plan to cut cocaine with flour and present it to the mob — delivered with complete confidence in this scheme.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke about their cluelessness — cutting drugs with flour as a mob-fooling strategy shows they have no idea how this world works. Not the most original premise but executed competently.

jokes.text: That's too much, huh? That's too much flour. We're dead! They're gonna kill us! We're dead 'cause of the flour. We're outta here.
jokes.setup: Dee puts in too much flour trying to cut the cocaine.
jokes.punchline: Their instant spiral from flour problem to 'We're dead 'cause of the flour' — the specific attribution of their death to the flour is the comedic payload.
jokes.explanation: 'We're dead 'cause of the flour' is a funny line — the specific attribution of their murder to the flour rather than the drug dealing is a good absurdist detail. Quick escalation well-executed.

jokes.text: It's just gonna be you and me and Peter Nincompoop.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee are planning to flee to the mountains.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's reference to 'Peter Nincompoop' — a third party in their escape plan who is apparently unknown to Dee.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Peter Nincompoop' as a name is inherently funny, but the setup — the casual inclusion of a mysterious third party in their escape plan — is what makes it. The name alone is a Charlie-specific detail (he would name a horse Peter Nincompoop). Perfectly economical and quotable.

jokes.text: Who's Peter Nincompoop? Huh? Huh? Oh, my God. How did that get here? I rode it here. What do you think?
jokes.setup: Dee asks who Peter Nincompoop is; Charlie acts confused and then a horse appears.
jokes.punchline: The horse is Peter Nincompoop. Charlie brought a horse to Dee's apartment and his response to 'How did that get here?' is 'I rode it here. What do you think?' — the most obvious possible answer to an impossible situation.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the great Sunny payoffs. The entire running gag about Charlie wanting a horse culminates in him simply... getting a horse and riding it to Dee's apartment, naming it Peter Nincompoop. 'I rode it here. What do you think?' is delivered with perfect Sunny logic — to Charlie, this is the obvious explanation. The character integration is extraordinary (only Charlie would do this), the structure of the reveal is excellent, and the payoff on the running gag is fully earned. This is what 8+ looks like.

jokes.text: We can't get outta here on that. We need a car. It's too obvious. It is? People will see... us and it.
jokes.setup: Charlie wants to escape on the horse.
jokes.punchline: Dee's objection that a horse is 'too obvious' as a getaway vehicle — as though the problem is detectability rather than the total insanity of escaping from the mob on horseback.
jokes.explanation: Dee's acceptance of the horse as a getaway vehicle in principle — her only objection being visibility — is a great beat. 'People will see... us and it' is a funny way to describe the problem.

jokes.text: You got a better chance without us, don't you, buddy? Okay. You know what, get outta here. Hah! Go, Peter Nincompoop! I miss you already!
jokes.setup: They decide the horse can't come with them in the car.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's heartfelt farewell to Peter Nincompoop — 'I miss you already!' — delivered with genuine emotion as the horse he's known for approximately ten minutes rides off.
jokes.explanation: 'I miss you already!' is an instantly quotable line. The emotional investment in a horse he literally just named and acquired, delivered with total sincerity, is both very funny and strangely touching. The character integration is exceptional — this is 100% Charlie. A great button on the best running gag in the episode.

jokes.text: I love you, Peter Nincompoop.
jokes.setup: Charlie has just said he misses Peter Nincompoop.
jokes.punchline: He adds 'I love you, Peter Nincompoop' — escalating the emotional investment in a horse he's releasing after moments of ownership.
jokes.explanation: The 'I love you' escalation after 'I miss you already' is the perfect button — Charlie's emotional arc with a horse he's known for minutes is complete. The name 'Peter Nincompoop' said with love is very funny. Great economy.

jokes.text: I'm gonna try and stay sharp here. That's mostly flour. But if we do enough of it, it should still work, right? Well, then, let's do a lot of it. Let's go!
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee are fleeing but have a bag of mostly-flour cocaine.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's scientific theory that if you do enough flour-cocaine, the trace cocaine will still work — and their immediate enthusiastic agreement to consume large amounts of flour.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's volume-compensation theory for diluted cocaine is exactly his kind of logic — wrong in an internally consistent way. 'Let's do a lot of it. Let's go!' is the right level of enthusiasm. Good.

jokes.text: That's a pop. That's a pop. That's a pop. Make it sexy. It has to be sexy. Otherwise, you don't eat. Okay? Frank, put the gun away. Oh, no. I'm goin' out, I'm goin' guns blazing.
jokes.setup: Frank is continuing to direct Dennis; the situation is deteriorating.
jokes.punchline: Frank's declaration that he's going out 'guns blazing' — responding to the existential threat of mob payback with theatrical bravado and a literal gun — while still giving performance notes.
jokes.explanation: Frank pulling a gun while still giving sex-work performance notes is a good beat — the incongruity of the two registers is funny. 'Guns blazing' as Frank's response to anything is on-brand.

jokes.text: Check it out. We got all the cocaine. Didn't get the cash. Got the cocaine. We might have bigger problems. We just pissed off the mob boss's wife because me and Dennis wouldn't bang her.
jokes.setup: The gang reconvenes at the bar.
jokes.punchline: Mac's summary of the situation — they have drugs but no cash and have offended the mob boss's wife by refusing to sleep with her — stated matter-of-factly as a 'bigger problem.'
jokes.explanation: Good situation summary comedy — the accumulation of absurd plot points stated calmly is functional Sunny.

jokes.text: When'd you get a gun? I went back to Bingo. Wow. I thought we said no guns though. That was before all the blow. You should've told me, because I've been carrying this thing around the entire time.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals he has a gun.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's injured complaint — 'You should've told me, because I've been carrying this thing around the entire time' — implying he also has a gun and has been holding it unnecessarily.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's parallel gun ownership being revealed only now — as a complaint about Frank's lack of communication — is a great beat. The implication that two of them have been secretly armed the whole time while worrying about their safety is very funny.

jokes.text: I'm gonna put this in my sock. And if the shit goes down, I'll pretend I'm tying my shoe. And I'll reach for some cigarettes. And when I ask for a light, we come out blastin'! Boom! Boom! Boom! Boom! Boom!
jokes.setup: The gang is making a plan for their mob confrontation.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's elaborate signal system for going guns-blazing — shoe-tying as the decoy, cigarette-reaching as the pivot, 'asking for a light' as the cue — is an absurdly complicated plan that would obviously fail.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's heist-movie gun plan is a great bit — the multi-step signal system (sock/shoe/cigarette/light/blast) escalates beautifully and his enthusiasm for the choreography is very funny. 'Boom! Boom! Boom! Boom! Boom!' as the endpoint is a great button. Strongly character-specific.

jokes.text: Oh! These guys. Hey. Ho. Hiya. All right. It's Friday. Youse guys got somethin' for me?
jokes.setup: The mob shows up to collect; the gang has been preparing an elaborate confrontation.
jokes.punchline: The mob guys arrive completely casually — 'Hey. Ho. Hiya.' — with zero menace, treating this as routine business. The anticipated showdown deflates immediately.
jokes.explanation: The deflation of the expected confrontation into 'Hey. Ho. Hiya.' is a solid anticlimax joke — all that preparation and the mob just rolls up like it's Friday (because it is Friday).

jokes.text: Has anybody got a light? Right here. Don't move! Put the guns down!
jokes.setup: Charlie's elaborate signal plan involved asking for a light as the cue to 'come out blasting.'
jokes.punchline: He actually does it — 'Has anybody got a light?' — immediately triggering the chaos, except nobody put the guns away so it's even more chaotic than planned.
jokes.explanation: The payoff on Charlie's elaborate signal plan is a great structural moment — he executes it exactly as described, and it immediately blows up into chaos. The callback is fully earned, the structure is clean, and the execution (someone actually gives him a light before all hell breaks loose) adds a perfect absurdist beat. Very strong joke.

jokes.text: Where'd you get the money? I sold Frank's pimp chalice. What? That's right, you son of a bitch. Thanks for bailing us out. Just like always. Goddamn it.
jokes.setup: Mac produces $25,000 to pay off the mob; the boss asks where it came from.
jokes.punchline: Mac sold Frank's pimp chalice — the ridiculous trophy Frank spent extravagantly on while refusing to pay the mob — and Frank's 'Goddamn it' is the right despairing button.
jokes.explanation: The pimp chalice callback is a fully earned payoff — it was introduced as an absurd waste of money, it becomes the solution to their problem. Frank's 'Goddamn it' at losing his prized possession while also being saved is the right note. Good structural comedy.

jokes.text: You guys, you gotta make it sexy... hips and nips. Otherwise, I'm not eatin'.
jokes.setup: The crisis is resolved; the mob boss is leaving.
jokes.punchline: Frank is still giving performance notes — 'hips and nips. Otherwise, I'm not eating' — mid-resolution of a mob standoff, completely unfazed.
jokes.explanation: 'Hips and nips' as Frank's governing aesthetic principle, repeated at an inappropriate moment, is very Frank. The persistence of his pimp-director mode through a mob confrontation is good character consistency.

jokes.text: It was nice doin' business with you guys. Hopefully, I'll never have to see you again. All righty. Sounds good. Sounds very good.
jokes.setup: The mob boss wraps up the encounter after being paid.
jokes.punchline: Both parties exchange polite farewells — 'sounds good, sounds very good' — as though this were any normal business transaction, and both sides mean 'I hope I never see you again' with equal sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The mutual courtesy between the gang and the mob is a good low-key button on the standoff. The functional politeness after drawn guns is quietly funny.

jokes.text: Explain to me why my wife is calling me telling me that one of Pussy Hands's friends tried to force himself on her. Oh! Oh! This guy? Oh! Oh! That's crazy! Enough with the 'Oh's'! I think that's insane. I have no idea what you're talking about.
jokes.setup: The mob boss brings up the Dennis/wife incident.
jokes.punchline: The 'Oh! Oh!' stalling tactic by the gang — buying time by making sounds — until the boss shuts them down with 'Enough with the Oh's!' The 'Pussy Hands' callback in the mouth of the mob boss is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: The 'Pussy Hands' name being used by the mob boss — establishing it has spread through the criminal organization — is a good running gag payoff. 'Enough with the Oh's!' is an excellent mob boss line. The gang's panic-stalling with just vowel sounds is good physical-verbal comedy.

jokes.text: Then I assume it was you, pinhead. No! It wasn't me! It wasn't me! Then who was it? You guys! I did it! And I made it so sexy!
jokes.setup: The mob boss is demanding to know who tried to sleep with his wife.
jokes.punchline: Dennis bursts in confessing — 'I did it! And I made it so sexy!' — with a kind of pride that is completely inappropriate given the context.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's confession is perfect — he doesn't just confess, he brags, and his primary concern is his sexual performance review ('I made it so sexy!'). 'I am the man!' is the kind of Dennis self-celebration that is both funny and totally in character. The juxtaposition of imminent danger and sexual pride is very Sunny.

jokes.text: Look at this. I've achieved total sexiness! I am the man! I made it so sexy. Get him. You got it, boss.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just confessed to sleeping with the mob boss's wife.
jokes.punchline: His triumphant declaration of 'total sexiness' as the mob boss orders his men to 'get him.' Dennis's obliviousness to the threat, replaced entirely by pride, is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'I've achieved total sexiness' is a great Dennis line — his primary KPI in life is sexiness, and even facing mob violence, he's satisfied he met it. 'Get him' as an immediate consequence is the right dark button.

jokes.text: It's so... it's so sexy. That's the thing. It's all hips and nips.
jokes.setup: Cricket is being dragged away by the mob.
jokes.punchline: Even as he's being removed by mob enforcers, Cricket can't stop enthusiastically explaining his sexual technique — 'it's all hips and nips' — his last words as a free man are artistic self-commentary.
jokes.explanation: Cricket's final declaration — 'it's all hips and nips' as he's dragged away — is a perfect button on his arc. His pride in his performance overrides all self-preservation. The phrase 'hips and nips' as a philosophy of seduction is memorable and quotable. Great running gag payoff.

jokes.text: It's so sexy. That's the thing. It's all hips and nips.
jokes.setup: Dennis is being dragged away by mob enforcers.
jokes.punchline: He's still explaining his sexiness methodology — 'it's all hips and nips' — while being physically removed by criminals.
jokes.explanation: Dennis evangelizing his sexiness technique while being dragged off is a great button — he's internalized Frank's philosophy so completely that he's teaching it even in crisis. 'Hips and nips' as his final words before being taken away is a perfect dark comedic image.

jokes.text: Do you guys have more blow? Yes! Get him outta here.
jokes.setup: Dennis is being taken away; the mob boss turns his attention to the gang.
jokes.punchline: The mob boss casually asks if they have more cocaine — transitioning seamlessly from ordering a beating to procurement — and Charlie's instant 'Yes!' suggests this is now their business relationship.
jokes.explanation: The mob boss's pivot from violence to procurement is a great dark-comedy beat — business is business. Charlie's immediate 'Yes!' with no hesitation suggests they've now inadvertently become mob drug suppliers. Good dark button on the whole arc.

jokes.text: They broke my legs but they didn't break my spirit / But I don't feel no pain 'cause I found more cocaine / Cocaine
jokes.setup: Episode ends with Cricket performing his musical — which is apparently a song about his own cocaine-fueled beat-down.
jokes.punchline: Cricket's show-stopping number summarizing his entire arc: broken legs, unbroken spirit, cocaine as the solution — delivered as triumphant musical theater.
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode-ending button. Cricket's descent has been the dark heart of the episode, and having him literally perform a musical about it — 'they broke my legs but they didn't break my spirit / but I don't feel no pain 'cause I found more cocaine' — is both hilarious and genuinely bleak. The character integration is exceptional: only Cricket, in this exact situation, could deliver this. The payoff on the musical running gag is complete. One of the episode's strongest moments.

tmdb_overview: While paying off their debt to the mob, Charlie and Dee try to find a way to make fake cocaine in order to fool them, while Dennis ranks in thousands of dollars being pimped out at the local country club. Mac realizes his position as a mob informant isn't being utilized to its full potential.
